formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 0.92. Factor = new area divided by old area = 117 divided by 127.2 = 0.92.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: A 9x13 covers 117 square inches and two 9-inch rounds cover 127.2. Divide 117 by 127.2 and the factor is 0.92.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 0.92, including the leavening. A recipe with 10 cups of batter becomes 9.2 cups.

howToSteps.name: Check the fill
howToSteps.text: Pour the scaled batter into a greased 9x13 pan. It should sit between half and two-thirds full, no higher than about 9.3 cups.

howToSteps.name: Bake as the recipe says
howToSteps.text: Same oven temperature, same bake time. Test the center with a toothpick, and give it a few more minutes if the center is still wet.

title: Two 9-Inch Rounds to 9x13 Converter
tutorial: A layer cake and a sheet cake are the same cake in different clothes. Two 9-inch rounds cover 127.2 square inches and a 9x13 covers 117, so the sheet pan is about 8 percent smaller. The factor is 117 divided by 127.2, which is 0.92. A two-layer recipe that makes 10 cups of batter becomes 9.2 cups in the sheet pan.

The gap is small enough that many bakers skip the scaling and pour the full two-layer batter into the 9x13. It works: the batter sits about 9 percent deeper, which is a small difference on a cake an inch and a half tall. Check the fill first, though. Two-thirds full in a 9x13 is about 9.3 cups, and a 10-cup recipe poured in whole is over the line. Scale it, or bake the extra cup as cupcakes.

If you do pour the full batter in, expect a few minutes longer in the oven. Deeper batter takes longer to set in the middle, and King Arthur puts the difference at up to 10 to 15 minutes for a meaningfully deeper bake. At 9 percent deeper the difference is small, more like 5 minutes, but the toothpick is the judge, not the clock.

A sheet cake is easier than a layer cake in every way except looks. One layer to frost instead of two layers plus sides, which means less frosting and less time. It travels in its own pan with a lid or foil over the top. It cuts into neat squares for a crowd, and the portions are easy to count. For a school bake sale or a potluck, the sheet cake is the right shape.

Bake at the same temperature and the same time as the recipe says. Both pans are 2 inches deep and the scaled batter sits at the same depth, so the middle sets on the same schedule. Test the center of the sheet cake with a toothpick, not the edge. A sheet cake hides a wet middle well, because the edges set long before the center does.
